I used to be a big fan of the platform because in 2020/2021 it was the only reasonable choice vs AWS/Azure/Snowflake. Today it suffers from feature creep and too many pivots & acquisitions. They are insanely bad at naming features.
Coming from hadoop, databricks is utopia. It's stable, fast, scales really well if you have massive datasets. The biggest gripe I have is how crazy expensive it is.
Databricks is the Jira of dealing with data. No one wants to use it, it sucks, there are too many features to try to appease all possible users but none of them particularly good.
They push Serverless so hard but there are SO MANY limitations and surprise gotchas. It's driving me absolutely insane.

No persist() so can't cache dataframes; no good way to get usage info programmatically; can't set Spark config easily (had to hack S3A credentials via options()); Unity Catalog only lets you mount external volumes matching your workspace's cloud provider, blocking cross-cloud setups.
They had an excellent Spark-as-a-Service product, at a time when you'd have better luck finding a leprechaun than a reliable self-hosted Spark instance in an enterprise environment.

Databricks' setup of spark saves an incredible amount of time on configuration and infra wiring. It's expensive and opinionated, but default configs give you much better performance out of the box than DIY, without fiddling with partitions.
Maybe unrelated but Databricks is the most annoying garbage I have ever had to use. It fascinates me how anyone uses it by choice.

Snowflake has much more advanced data security - table, column, row level security, dynamic data masking, and zero-copy cloning. Databricks security seems lacking - just table level, only in SQL and Spark, none in R. I liked the Databricks UI and integrated visualizations though.

Not only is Databricks a deplorable company when it comes to HR, but their product is terrible. I really don't get what it's all about. Much rather spin up my own python notebook with my own underlying data storage.

My experience with 'Scala at scale' was extremely unsatisfactory and I found Databricks to give very unhelpful responses to basic performance problems arising from the intersection of Scala and Spark, bordering on gaslighting.
We've been moving our workflows out of Databricks to PostgreSQL to save a ton.

Databricks coined the 'Delta lake' concept and are still (just about) leading the way, but Fabric has the potential to take away marketshare. Databricks need to improve their 'serverless SQL' offering, and add a serious 'data warehouse' component alongside the lake.

A former fan says that in 2020/2021 Databricks was the only reasonable choice compared to AWS, Azure, or Snowflake for building data platforms. Today it suffers from feature creep and too many pivots and acquisitions, and it is 'insanely bad at naming features'.
'Coming from hadoop, databricks is utopia. It's stable, fast, scales really well if you have massive datasets.' The biggest gripe is how crazy expensive it is.

If you're going to use Spark, Databricks' setup saves an incredible amount of time otherwise wasted on configuring storage, compute, pipelines, unified access, and VPNs. It's expensive and opinionated, but cheaper than the data engineers needed to fight Spark OOM errors. Its default configs perform much better out of the box than DIY, with no fiddling with partitions to stabilize medium workloads.

'Databricks is the Jira of dealing with data.' No one wants to use it, and it has too many features trying to appease all users, none particularly good. There are substantially better options now, and the commenter would never use it by choice.

Databricks pushes Serverless hard, but it has many gotchas: no persist() to cache dataframes, no good programmatic usage info, and Spark config can't be set (S3A credentials needed obscure options() workarounds). Unity Catalog can't mount external volumes from a different cloud's storage. The Snowflake-style VARIANT type caused even more pain.
Serverless tends to be notably more expensive: '4-5x the price for less features.' Another user replied that the new cost-optimized mode is very promising, though.

In the late 2010s Databricks had an excellent Spark-as-a-Service product, at a time when a reliable self-hosted Spark instance in an enterprise was beyond most IT teams. The first-party hyperscaler offerings were relatively spartan.
'I've used both products in production. Both are good++.' (Databricks and Snowflake.) The commenter never chose one over the other based on benchmark speed on an arbitrary dataset.

A big benefit of Snowflake or Databricks over traditional tech is pay-as-you-go pricing. Scaling a licensed EC2-based tool was painful, whereas with Databricks 'we could just scale it up and update our opex estimate.'

In a PoC, Databricks security seemed lacking: table-level only, and only in SQL and Spark, with no security at all in R. Snowflake has row/column security and masking. Using it for industrialized processing was price-impractical versus AWS Glue. The commenter really liked Databricks' UI and integrated visualizations.
Their Databricks PoC ended over a price quote: management found the license cost reasonable until told it excluded EC2 costs. The real cost would be at least twice as much.
Databricks pushes 'open', but keeps the optimizations needed to run at scale proprietary. Users are steered toward its tech to transform data into Parquet/Delta, then query with Photon/SQL.
At one F50 company, Databricks runs just one or two production projects someone built. Neither Databricks nor Snowflake is 'the chosen tool' there.
'Databricks is the most annoying garbage I have ever had to use. It fascinates me how anyone uses it by choice.'
A company with 2PB+ in Cloudera chose not to move to the cloud and Databricks. Instead it built its own analytics platform with Iceberg, Trino, and Superset, saving 5X on costs.
'Their product is terrible. I really don't get what it's all about.' The commenter would much rather spin up their own Python notebook and own underlying data storage.

A user's experience with Scala and Spark on Databricks at scale was very unsatisfactory, and Databricks gave very unhelpful responses to basic performance problems, 'bordering on gaslighting'. Memory bloat was pernicious: large data had to be handled very carefully to avoid huge memory footprints and hard-to-debug cascading failures.
'We've been moving our workflows out of Databricks to PostgreSQL to save a ton.'
